text.p: Mortgage-backed securities prices were weaker late in the session as the market awaited July retail sales and producer price index data due Wednesday.
Treasuries closed weaker ahead of the retail sales data, reflecting some investor anxiety that the data might indicate an economy that is heating up.

Mortgage-backed securities spreads to Treasuries tightened as Treasury security prices weakened, participants said. They said MBS spreads had been wider earlier in the session when Treasury prices firmed on news that the Richmond Fed July manufacturing shipments index fell to -10 from 15 in June.
The 10-year Treasury note was 8/32 lower at 97 31/32 to yield 6.40 percent.

Current coupon Government National Mortgage Association mortgage securities were 10/32 weaker at 100 17/32 to yield 7.46 percent. Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp 7.5 percent coupons were off 7/32 at 100 21/32 to yield 7.39 percent. And, Fannie Mae 7.5 percent coupons were 7/32 lower at 100 27/32 to yield 7.39 percent.
Fletcher said investors were trying to determine whether the correction in Treasury prices seen in recent sessions portended a bear market or if it merely is bull market correcction.
"The real question people are asking is whether this a sign that a bear trend has begun," said Fletcher, noting that the reaction to the retail sales data "will begin to give us an answer."
According to economists surveyed by Reuters, July retail sales were expected to have risen 0.7 percent. Excluding autos, retail sales are expected to have risen 0.5 percent in July.

The July producer price index report was also due Wednesday -- economists surveyed by Reuters expected producer prices to rise 0.1 percent -- but the retail sales report was expected to enjoy heightened attention because it could offer a measure of consumer demand.

How Treasury prices react to the data could determine the performance of mortgage securities this week, participants said. If Treasuries shrug off the sales and inflation data, then mortgage investors are sure to breath a sigh of relief.
Data bolstering Treasury prices could spark prepayment fears among mortgage-backed investors if it looks like a return to 6.00 percent on the 10-year Treasury note may be imminent.

Lower rates could inspire home-owner refinancings. Levels seen earlier this summer prompted discussion about which mortgage loan pools were prepayable as well as some down-in-coupon trading or movement out of mortgage securities into Treasuries.
